extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy; philosophers and general educated public
extracted.subtask_description: Lecture-text exposition of the pragmatic method and a genetic/instrumental theory of truth: how to settle metaphysical disputes by tracing practical consequences and how to judge ideas by their workability and relation to experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic method (interpret notions by tracing practical consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: THE PRAGMATIC METHOD: try to interpret each notion by tracing its respective practical consequences. What difference would it practically make to anyone if this notion rather than that notion were true? If no practical difference can be traced, the alternatives mean practically the same thing and dispute is idle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the squirrel anecdote: resolving 'does the man go round the squirrel?' depends on what one practically means by 'going round.' Use the test of concrete practical consequences to settle metaphysical disputes that otherwise seem interminable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of ideas via conduct they prescribe (Peirce's principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: To develop a thought's meaning, determine what conduct it is fitted to produce: that conduct is for us its sole significance. The tangible fact at the root of thought-distinctions is possible differences of practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peirce's formulation: beliefs are rules for action; attain clearness by considering conceivable effects (sensations, reactions) the idea may involve. Applied examples include scientific questioning of what experimental differences would follow from rival theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical-difference test for collapsing disputes in science
rubrics_metrics.description: If rival scientific views would produce no different experimental facts or conduct, the controversy is unreal and should not be pursued as metaphysically significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ostwald's tautomerous-chemistry example: if no experiment could distinguish two accounts, the quarrel is futile. Similarly, the radium/helium example shows how experimental consequences (discovery of helium) resolved seeming contradictions with conservation principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as instrumental/usefulness (ideas true insofar as they help us relate experience)
rubrics_metrics.description: THAT IDEAS ... BECOME TRUE JUST IN SO FAR AS THEY HELP US TO GET INTO SATISFACTORY RELATION WITH OTHER PARTS OF OUR EXPERIENCE. Truth means the power of ideas to work: to summarize, to link experiences, to simplify and to get about among experiences by conceptual shortcuts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Called the 'instrumental' view of truth (championed by Dewey, Schiller). An idea's truth is judged by its success in helping us act and navigate experience — 'true in so far forth, true INSTRUMENTALLY.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Theories as instruments, not final answers
rubrics_metrics.description: THEORIES THUS BECOME INSTRUMENTS, NOT ANSWERS TO ENIGMAS, IN WHICH WE CAN REST. Theories are programs for more work and indications of ways existing realities may be changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theories should be used actively (to 'make nature over again' when needed) rather than treated as terminuses that close inquiry. They 'limber up' thought and are judged by practical fruit, not by their supposed finality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-intellectualist orientation: favor concreteness, adequacy, facts, action, power
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn away from abstraction, verbal solutions, bad a priori reasons, fixed principles, closed systems and pretended absolutes; turn towards concreteness and adequacy, towards facts, towards action, and towards power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pragmatism endorses an empiricist temper that privileges practical adequacy and intimacy with facts over abstract, closed, or purely rationalistic systems. This is presented as a methodological preference for philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assimilation criterion (problem of maxima and minima) for adopting new ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: A new idea is adopted as 'true' to the degree that it preserves the existing stock of opinions with a minimum of disturbance while accommodating new experience — the 'problem of maxima and minima.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals are conservative; truth grows by grafting new ideas onto old beliefs so as to minimize jolt. The best/newest theories are those that most felicitously mediate between old opinions and new facts (examples: how belief about radium was reconciled by discovering helium).

rubrics_metrics.name: Loyalty to older truths (historical/genealogical constraint on belief-change)
rubrics_metrics.description: Loyalty to older truths is the controlling principle in belief revision; most changes conserve as much of the prior system as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to account for the role of older truths is a common criticism leveled against pragmatism. The growth of truth is presented as a historical, cumulative process in which older beliefs constrain and shape acceptance of novelties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genetic/humanistic theory of truth (truth as human-centered and contingent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reasons why we call things true are the reasons why they are true: 'to be true' means to perform the marriage-function of linking previous parts of experience with newer parts. Purely objective, incorrigible truth independent of human needs is denied or downplayed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schiller's 'Humanism' and the pragmatist claim that truth has a human genealogy: truths may petrify with antiquity but remain historically contingent. The transformation of logical/mathematical ideas demonstrates plasticity of even ancient truths.
